full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This appeal by special leave is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division, setting aside, in exercise of the powers under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an order made by the first Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca, rejecting the prayer of the respondent for amendment of the additional written statement filed by the said respondent in a suit instituted by the appellants for declaration of their title. 

 2. The appellants instituted the suit as plaintiffs on 26-10-67 in the first Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca against Bangladesh, the respondent for declaration of their title to the land in suit and also for declaration that a certain notice, issued by the Member, Board of Revenue, upon the plaintiffs and all subsequent actions taken by him were illegal, void and without jurisdiction on the allegations that the suit land was originally the khas land of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate which settled the same in 1344 B.S. with some of the plaintiffs processors and others in raiyati right, that during the survey operation under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the respondent, whereupon an application was filed on behalf of the appellants for correction of the record of rights under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, that the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dacca recognised them as the tenants on the basis of their settlement and long standing possession and realized rent from them, but that the Board of Revenue, by a notice dated 15-6- 67 purported to cancel the recognition already granted to the plaintiffs and their predecessors. 

 3. The respondent filed a written statement on 13-11-68 denying the allegation of settlement as pleaded in the plaint and stated, inter alia, that the suit land was vacant land in possession of the Bhawal Raj Estate, that it was acquired by the Government as excess khas land of Bhawal Raj Estate under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 4. On 9-12-70 the appellants filed a voluminous petition for amendment of the plaint, consisting of about 15 pages (the original plaint being of about 4 pages only) wherein it was stated, inter alia, that the disputed land has been acquired under the provisions of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 by the respondent, taking the land to be the land of the old tenants or their transferees, in the Land Acquisition Case No.41/64-65 of the Dacca Collectorate, that compensation for the said lands had been paid in part and the acquiring authority was entitled to possession thereof on payment of the compensation according to law, that in 1967 the Board of Revenue issued a notice purporting to cancel the recognition of the appellants or their predecessors as tenants, and that in March, 1968 a notice for eviction of certain persons from the disputed lands was issued by the respondent under the East Bengal Act X of 1953. It was stated in the said petition for amendment of the plaint that all the facts were not properly stated in the original plaint of the suit which was deficient in certain details and a prayer was made to accept the said petition as a part of the plaint. By an order dated 30-12-70 the said petition for amendment of the plaint was made a part of the plaint and an additional written statement was filed by the respondent on 6-7-71 in respect of the said amended plaint. 

 5. It appears that on 13-1-73 an application was filed by the respondent for amendment of the additional written statement on the averments that some bonafide mistake crept in to paragraph 10 of the additional written statement which required rectification by way of amendment. By this petition the respondent wanted to delete the following statement as made in the said paragraph: 

 "With the requisition and acquisition the property vested in the Government and the Govt. is entitled to take the possession of the same on payment of provisional compensation to the owners and the real owners have been paid compensation. " 

 "Some of the plaintiffs have been paid compensation as per provisional award prepared by the Land Acquisition Collector before the receipt of the cancellation order of the Senior Member, Board of Revenue cancelling the entry in C.S. Plot No. 401 in the Collector's Khatian in the record of rights. The plaintiffs are not entitled to take advantage of this wrong payment, as the plaintiffs have acquired no right, title or interest over the suit property nor their alleged vendors had any right, title or interest over the suit property." 

 "The defense wants to delete some admissions made in the written statement by way of amendment. This will, no doubt, prejudice the right of the plaintiffs and should not be allowed at this stage of the suit and this would have the effect of getting out of defendant's admission in the pleading." 

 The respondent moved the High Court Division against the said order of rejection of the prayer for amendment, the additional written statement under section 115 of the Cede, upon which a rule was issued and the learned Judges by their judgment dated 5-7-73 made the rule absolute and allowed the respondent's application for amendment of the additional written statement on the view that the proposed amendment of the additional written statement would help the determination of the real question in controversy between the parties. 

 10. It will appear that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge misdirected himself in approaching the question of justifiability of the amendment from a wrong point of view. It appears from his order that his refusal was dictated by the consideration that the defendant by the amendment was trying to get out of its admission and that the plaintiffs being deprived of the advantage of such an admission would be prejudiced. This consideration, which impelled the learned Subordinate Judge to refuse the amendment as has been referred to above, is absolutely irrelevant. The Court concerned shall have to find out, according to the terms of the rule whether the proposed amendment is likely to facilitate the determination of the real questions in controversy. The main dispute in the suit appears to arise from the averments of the plaintiffs on the one hand that they had acquired right, title and interest in respect of the disputed land by virtue of the alleged settlement granted by the original proprietors, namely, Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate, and the averments of the defendant, on the other hand, that there was no such settlement by the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate in favour of some of the plaintiffs or their predecessors and seems others. The real question of controversy seems to be the creation or existence of the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs in respect of the disputed land by virtue of the said settlement. 

 11. What the defendant wanted to amend was what was stated by it to be a bonafide mistake in making the indirect admission of title of the plaintiffs and to bring the statement in paragraph 10 of the additional written statement in conformity to the rest of the written statement as such admission as was made in paragraph 10, does not appear to have been consistent with the other allegations of the defendant made in the additional written statement and the deletion of such an admission is likely to pinpoint the real question of controversy in a more certain and definite manner. The question of prejudice is absolutely beside the point. It may be pointed out that the admission, as was made in paragraph 10 of the written statement, is a kind of inference of law and an admission on the point of a legal position is not binding upon any person and withdrawal of such an admission is not likely to prejudice anybody. If the factual position that there was no settlement in favour of the plaintiffs or their predecessor is established the question of entitlement of the Govt. to take possession of the property, which was sought to be acquired under the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, would not at all arise because the original right of the Government, if any accrued on the acquisition of the khas land of the Bhawal Raj Estate under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, would not be affected in any way by a misconceived procedure taken under the Emergency Requisition of Property Act of 1948. 

 The power of amendment of pleadings as provided in Order 6, rule 17 of the Code is certainly a matter of discretion but the court shall have to exercise such discretion judicially in conformity with the terms of the aforesaid provision. If the learned Subordinate Judge failed to exercise his discretion to allow the amendment of the written statement from absolutely a wrong point of view it would certainly by a failure on his part to exercise the jurisdiction as was conferred upon him by the aforesaid provision of Order 6, rule 17 of the Code. The learned Judges of the High Court Division appear to have taken the correct review in the matter and rightly exercised their revisional jurisdiction in setting aside the order of the learned Subordinate Judge.
